summary: Decision-only commit; no tests staged, so the review is of whether the recorded decision lets M4.10c/d write tests that KILL the mutations it names. Four of the five mutations it names are killable and one is well specified (the depth-two Math::max warning is the best test guidance in the commit). The fifth is not: ADR-0036 asserts the once-per-delta placement is invisible to every M4 test and 'passes both new goldens'. Measured false against the tree -- BatchedCommitDeltaTest builds a 3-segment/3-pod delta at T0, GoldenChainEntryTest carries a 2-segment batched golden with byte-identical re-encode asserted, and BatchingSequencerTest:259 asserts a 2-pod delta hasSize(2). The claim tells the M4.10c author not to write the one fixture that kills the mutation. R4a remedy verified applied; the two-histories rendering verified accurate against DefaultIngest.java:349; R4b and R4e confirmed still minor.

findings.title: The ADR tells M4.10c that no M4 test can kill the once-per-delta placement mutation. Measured false: three tests in the tree already build multi-segment deltas at T0/T1.
findings.claim_as_written: ADR:99-103 'The placement is load-bearing and M4-invisible: commitAll is the primitive, every production delta in M4 is single-segment, so a once-per-delta field round-trips, passes both new goldens and is byte-equivalent today'. backlog.md:123 'every M4 delta is single-segment so the two placements are byte-equivalent today and only M5 tells them apart.'
findings.measured: The PRODUCTION half is defensible -- M4.10c's own notes record that nothing constructs a BatchingSequencer outside its own test. The TEST half is false. format/src/test/java/binjava/format/BatchedCommitDeltaTest.java:41-45 builds a THREE-segment CommitDelta from bins/pod-a, pod-b and pod-c and asserts each segment's own key and firstOffset survive the round trip, at T0, with no M5. format/src/test/java/binjava/format/GoldenChainEntryTest.java:76-84 decodes golden/chain-delta-batched-v1.bin -- a TWO-segment delta with distinct keys -- asserts containsExactly on both SegmentCommits and then asserts encode() is byte-identical. sequencer/src/test/java/binjava/sequencer/BatchingSequencerTest.java:259-262 calls commitAll(List.of(from("pod0",0), from("pod1",0))) and asserts delta.segments() hasSize(2). The ADR also contradicts itself: its own 'Which formats change' says 'Both delta encodings change, VERSION_DELTA and the kinded batch -- both paths, or neither', and the kinded batch path IS the multi-segment one whose only golden is multi-segment.
findings.failure_scenario: MUTATION: encode the idempotency triple ONCE PER DELTA (a single (podId, incarnationId, flushSeq) field beside `sequence`) instead of once per SegmentCommit. The M4.10c author, having been told the two placements are indistinguishable before M5 and that the mutation 'passes both new goldens', writes the cheaper one-field encoding and builds the new kinded golden with a single triple -- or with the same triple repeated on both segments, which the claim actively invites. Every new test is green. The shape then drops every pod but one on M5's first forwarded multi-pod batch, which is the defect the ADR itself names one clause later. The mutation is killable TODAY and cheaply: give BatchedCommitDeltaTest's existing three-segment fixture three DIFFERENT triples and assert decoded.segments().get(1) and .get(2) each carry their OWN podId/incarnationId/flushSeq; under the once-per-delta encoding all three decode to one triple and the assertion fails. The precedent for exactly this fixture shape is already written down in M4.8a's notes ('a fixture of at least 6 streams and 2 pods, and distinct non-default values in every field').
findings.remedy: Deletion, not rewriting: strike 'passes both new goldens' from the ADR and 'only M5 tells them apart' from backlog.md:123. Keep 'every production delta in M4 is single-segment' (it is true and it is the reason the placement is easy to get wrong) and keep the per-SegmentCommit requirement. Optionally replace the deleted clause with the discriminating fixture, since it exists: 'a multi-segment delta with DISTINCT triples per segment separates the two placements at T0 -- BatchedCommitDeltaTest already carries the three-segment fixture.'

findings.title: The second history's route label supplies a caller-side discriminator that Sequencer.commit's own javadoc denies.
findings.claim_as_written: 'and a flushSeq consumed by DefaultIngest's unconditional flushSeq++ on a commit that then threw (nothing applied, so a re-flush is safe)'.
findings.measured: The mechanism is accurate: DefaultIngest.java:349 evaluates flushSeq++ as an argument, so it is consumed before commit is invoked and the catch at the end of flushLocked does not roll it back -- 'density is over ISSUED flushes, not applied ones' is correct, and both histories do reach the refuse branch. What is not accurate is the parenthetical's universal. sequencer/src/main/java/binjava/sequencer/Sequencer.java:86-89 documents the seam's only failure channel as '@throws IOException the store was unreachable -- AMBIGUOUS, so the commit may or may not have landed'. A commit that threw may therefore have applied, in which case the history is the FIRST one, not the second. flushLocked's catch is also wider than the commit call (IOException | RuntimeException over the whole block, including the code after a successful commit), so 'threw' does not imply 'did not apply' even locally.
findings.failure_scenario: MUTATION: implement M4.10d's caller rule as 're-flush iff the previous attempt threw'. This is exactly what the parenthetical licenses -- it hands the caller the discriminator the paragraph's own headline says does not exist -- and it rescues the blanket rule the paragraph is trying to forbid. A test written from it (fail the commit, re-flush, assert the records are committed once) is GREEN, because a test fake throws without applying. In production the ambiguous IOException case applies and then throws, and one set of records holds two sets of committed offsets: the precise outcome the paragraph's last sentence warns about, reintroduced by its own illustration. Remedy is a five-word deletion -- drop 'nothing applied, so a re-flush is safe' and let the contrast rest on the outcome partition (applied / not applied), which is what the sequencer genuinely cannot see. NOT recommended for a further round on its own; fold into T1's edit if T1 is fixed.

findings.title: 'REFUSE with a distinguishable error' still names no observable, and the surrounding text moving has raised its weight rather than lowered it.
findings.measured: Sequencer.commit declares only `throws IOException` (Sequencer.java:91), documented as AMBIGUOUS-and-retry (:86-89). There is no second channel, so 'distinguishable' is not constructible at the seam as it stands. Since R4, M4.10d's backlog row (backlog.md:124) has GAINED the answer-or-refuse rule ('else REFUSED'), so a row now prescribes a behaviour whose observable is unspecified.
findings.failure_scenario: MUTATION: make the refuse branch throw a bare IOException with any message. A M4.10d test asserting refusal has nothing to assert on but an exception message substring -- assertThatThrownBy(...).hasMessageContaining("replay") -- so changing the message to anything else, or throwing the same type from an unrelated store failure inside the same call, is indistinguishable from a correct refusal. The test constrains a string, not a behaviour. I still recommend NOT fixing this here: the remedy is a typed exception or an Optional-shaped return, which is a seam change M4.10d owns and cannot be discharged by a sentence in an ADR. Recording it so it is harvested at the milestone boundary.

findings.title: The 32-bytes-per-pod figure still bounds nothing, because the assertion it leans on counts streams and carries no pods at all.
findings.measured: format/src/test/java/binjava/format/CheckpointTest.java:153-169: the test is aCheckpointAt1600StreamsStaysNearItsSTATEDSize, its loop is `for (int n = 0; n < 1600; n++)` over STREAMS, its comment says '~38 KiB at 1,600 streams', and its assertion is isLessThan(64 * 1024). It adds no pods. So '32 bytes per pod does not approach the remainder' is a comparison against a ~26 KiB headroom with no pod count on the other side; it happens to hold below roughly 830 pods, a number the ADR never states.
findings.failure_scenario: MUTATION: store something per pod that is NOT fixed-width -- the segment key the ADR explicitly rejects at up to MAX_KEY_BYTES (verified 1024, SegmentKey.java:62). No test in the tree fails, because the only size assertion has zero pods in its fixture, and the ADR's own sentence reads as though it had already been checked against one. The remedy is one clause naming the pod count the bound is claimed at, so M4.10c has a fixture arity to write to (M4.8a's notes already do this correctly for streams). I continue to recommend NOT fixing this here -- it is decoration in Consequences, not a normative rule, and M4.10c is where the fixture is actually built. Contrast M4.46's notes, which handle a number correctly by scoping it ('the 175/200 on Clock.systemUTC() is an artifact of a fixture whose appends fall inside one millisecond, NOT an 87% production rate').

findings.location: sequencer/src/main/java/binjava/sequencer/Sequencer.java:86-89 (not touched by this commit; falsified by it)
findings.title: A fact this ADR falsifies survives in the seam javadoc a M4.10d author reads first, and no row owns the fix.
findings.measured: Sequencer.commit's @throws still reads 'Retrying with the same {@code (podId, flushSeq)} is safe only from M4.10'. ADR-0036 decides that the bare pair cannot carry idempotency at all; after M4.10d, retrying on the pair will not be safe -- it needs the incarnation. Neither the M4.10c row (backlog.md:123) nor the M4.10d row (:124) nor either notes section names this javadoc. M4.10d's notes DO name the other duplicate (CheckpointWriter's Math::max comment), which is what makes the omission visible.
findings.failure_scenario: MUTATION: implement M4.10d's dedup keyed on (podId, flushSeq), as the seam javadoc still instructs. That is the original defect -- a restarted pod reissues 0,1,2 and dedup SUPPRESSES REAL COMMITS -- and the ADR's stated primary harm. The M4.10d row does say 'keyed on (podId, incarnationId, flushSeq)', so a reader of the row is safe; a reader of the interface is not, and the interface is what a caller reads (that seam's own javadoc argues exactly this at :81-86 about a different settled question). Cheapest remedy inside this commit's scope: one clause in M4.10c's or M4.10d's notes naming Sequencer.java:86-89 as a site the change must update, so it has an owner. This is the M4.10a baselines failure mode ('fixing one copy of a fact and missing its duplicates') and is worth a line, not a round.

confirmations: R4a remedy verified by grep over docs/: the sentence 'Refusing neither duplicates nor suppresses: nothing applied under that key, and the caller can re-flush.' is ABSENT from the tree. It was deleted, not rewritten. The answer-or-refuse rule at ADR:60-69 is intact and unweakened.

The two-histories rendering at backlog-notes.md:286-294 is accurate to the R4 finding on the mechanism. Verified DefaultIngest.java:349 consumes flushSeq via an unconditional flushSeq++ evaluated before commit is invoked, and flushLocked's catch does not roll it back; 'density is over ISSUED flushes, not applied ones' follows. Both histories genuinely reach the refuse branch under ADR:52-69 (lastApplied=6, replay of 5 detected, pointed delta does not carry 5, refuse). The conclusion -- a blanket refuse-then-re-flush is unsafe and a test written from it is green -- is correct and is the right thing to have handed to M4.10d. One route label overclaims: see T2.

The strongest test guidance in the commit is backlog-notes.md:296-301, and it should be preserved verbatim: it names a mutation (carry pods.merge(podId, flushSeq, Math::max) across incarnations), then names the fixture depth that kills it. Verified: CheckpointWriter.java:126-129's comment argues for max-never-put; carried across incarnations, the first post-restart commit is accepted because the incarnation differs while the slot keeps the old high watermark, and the SECOND (flushSeq 1 <= old high) is refused. A depth-one test -- one restart, one commit -- passes. Naming the required depth is exactly what stops that.

Quotations spot-checked against source and all accurate: the Hop javadoc 'are never GET at all' (ChainReplay.java:50, and it IS Hop's javadoc); SegmentPublisher's 'unique WITHOUT coordination' (:137) with an unconditional store.put (:141) and an instance AtomicLong sequence (:53); CheckpointWriter's 'the only place the writer can see' (:105); MAX_KEY_BYTES = 1024 (SegmentKey.java:62); CheckpointTest's 64 KiB / 1,600 streams / ~38 KiB (:153-169); glossary.md:15 for producer as the record supplier; and M3.0's golden sentence (backlog-done.md:93).

All six acceptance properties in M4.10b's notes are answered by the ADR, including the one the packet flags as the opposite-direction hazard: a pre-change checkpoint yields an empty window, and the ADR chooses ACCEPT with the reason stated (refusing would suppress legitimate commits) and a bound (it closes at the first post-upgrade checkpoint). ADR-0031 is correctly demoted to a precondition at :78-80 and :157-161.

No existing assertion was weakened: the staged diff touches docs only (verified git diff --cached --stat -- six files, all under docs/ and baselines/). No test file changed, so the check-test-integrity inversion cannot apply here.
landable_note: Not landable as staged, on T1 alone. T1 is one deletion of two clauses; everything else in the commit is sound and T2-T5 are minors I recommend recording rather than fixing. If the author argues T1 rather than fixing it, the argument has to account for GoldenChainEntryTest's existing two-segment batched golden and the ADR's own 'both paths, or neither', because 'passes both new goldens' is a claim about tests and not about production traffic.
